metadata.title: System Design Reading Materials - Detailed Topic-wise Curriculum
metadata.purpose: Prepare candidates for system design interviews and production architecture reviews with detailed reading modules, diagram prompts, failure modes, tradeoffs and practice labs.
metadata.enhancements: Each module includes topic_specific_deep_dive with concrete notes, interview questions, advanced variations and senior-level signals.

modules.topic: System design interview framing and answer structure
modules.learning_objective: Master System design interview framing and answer structure deeply enough to design, critique, operate and evolve production systems under medium-to-hard interview constraints.
modules.overview: This module teaches System design interview framing and answer structure as a system-design capability, not as a vocabulary item. Study it by connecting requirements, scale assumptions, data ownership, failure behavior, security boundaries and operational controls. A strong answer explains when the technique is useful, when it fails, what it costs, and how the design changes as traffic, teams and reliability targets grow.
modules.role_application: In interviews, System design interview framing and answer structure usually appears when the candidate must move from a vague product problem to an executable architecture. Use it to justify boundaries, choose data stores, define APIs, calculate scale, and explain the tradeoff between correctness, latency, availability, cost and team ownership.
reading_path: Start from the problem and user-visible requirements.
Quantify scale and reliability before choosing services.
Design the baseline architecture and explicitly name state ownership.
Stress the design with failures, overload, stale data, security threats and cost constraints.
Finalize with diagrams, metrics, migration path and open risks.

details: Define the problem that System design interview framing and answer structure solves and the failure it prevents.
Identify the primary state owner, the scaling unit, and the consistency expectation.
Separate product invariants from implementation preferences before choosing technology.
Write the one-sentence tradeoff: what becomes easier and what becomes harder if you use this design.
Trace the happy path for System design interview framing and answer structure from client request to durable state and response.
Trace retries, duplicate messages, stale reads, authorization failures, overload and regional failures.
Map every state change to a persistence, cache, queue, index or external dependency.
Connect each decision to one of the constraints: volume, latency, availability, correctness, security or cost.
Define ownership: team, service, database, on-call path and escalation path.
Define operational signals: golden metrics, logs, traces, saturation metrics and business KPIs.
Define protection mechanisms: rate limits, quotas, circuit breakers, backpressure, authz checks and audit trails.
Define evolution strategy: schema changes, versioning, backfills, migrations and rollback.
Start with requirements and explicit assumptions instead of a memorized architecture.
Estimate scale quickly enough to identify the first bottleneck.
Draw the simplest working design, then harden it for scale, failures and operations.
State tradeoffs and rejected alternatives; this is where seniority is visible.

diagrams_to_draw.purpose: Expose operational controls for System design interview framing and answer structure: health checks, alerts, fallbacks and rollback paths.

Draw the critical-path sequence diagram for System design interview framing and answer structure; mark every synchronous call and timeout.

Write a postmortem scenario for System design interview framing and answer structure: choose a realistic outage, root cause it, and modify the architecture.
practice_drills: Explain System design interview framing and answer structure in 90 seconds to a staff engineer.
Explain System design interview framing and answer structure in 90 seconds to a product manager without jargon.
Name three alternatives to the main approach and one reason each alternative may be better.
Choose one metric that proves System design interview framing and answer structure is working and one metric that proves it is failing.
mastery_check: Can you draw System design interview framing and answer structure from memory and explain every arrow?
Can you quantify how System design interview framing and answer structure affects latency, storage, cost or availability?
Can you explain the migration path from a simpler design to this design?
Can you identify the worst failure mode and the first alert that would catch it?
Can you defend the design against an interviewer pushing for a different data store, API style or deployment model?
assessment_prompts: Design a production-ready subsystem where System design interview framing and answer structure is the central design challenge.
Compare two designs for System design interview framing and answer structure: one optimized for low latency and one optimized for correctness.
Given 10x traffic, 5x data size and one regional outage, revise the architecture for System design interview framing and answer structure.
Find the hidden single point of failure in a proposed System design interview framing and answer structure architecture.

study_notes: Always write assumptions before architecture; otherwise the design is untestable.
Use diagrams to communicate scope and boundaries, not artistic detail.
A senior answer includes risks, alternatives and migration strategy.
questions_to_answer_before_interview: What is the source of truth for System design interview framing and answer structure?
Which operation becomes the bottleneck first for System design interview framing and answer structure: read, write, fanout, storage, network, or coordination?
What are the exact consistency and freshness guarantees users need for System design interview framing and answer structure?
How does System design interview framing and answer structure behave when a dependency is slow, unavailable, overloaded, or returning partial errors?
Which metric, alert and dashboard would prove System design interview framing and answer structure is healthy in production?

System design interview framing and answer structure under a regional outage
System design interview framing and answer structure with stricter privacy or compliance requirements
senior_level_signals: States assumptions and constraints before drawing.
Names rejected alternatives and explains why they were rejected.
Separates data plane, control plane and operational plane where relevant.
Designs for migration, rollback, observability and ownership.
Quantifies tradeoffs instead of saying it depends.

A strong answer explains when the technique is useful, when it fails, what it costs, and how the design changes as traffic, teams and reliability targets grow.
modules.role_application: In interviews, Architecture decision records and design docs usually appears when the candidate must move from a vague product problem to an executable architecture. Use it to justify boundaries, choose data stores, define APIs, calculate scale, and explain the tradeoff between correctness, latency, availability, cost and team ownership.
reading_path: Start from the problem and user-visible requirements.
Quantify scale and reliability before choosing services.
Design the baseline architecture and explicitly name state ownership.
Stress the design with failures, overload, stale data, security threats and cost constraints.
Finalize with diagrams, metrics, migration path and open risks.

details: Define the problem that Architecture decision records and design docs solves and the failure it prevents.
Identify the primary state owner, the scaling unit, and the consistency expectation.
Separate product invariants from implementation preferences before choosing technology.
Write the one-sentence tradeoff: what becomes easier and what becomes harder if you use this design.
Trace the happy path for Architecture decision records and design docs from client request to durable state and response.
Trace retries, duplicate messages, stale reads, authorization failures, overload and regional failures.
Map every state change to a persistence, cache, queue, index or external dependency.
Connect each decision to one of the constraints: volume, latency, availability, correctness, security or cost.
Define ownership: team, service, database, on-call path and escalation path.
Define operational signals: golden metrics, logs, traces, saturation metrics and business KPIs.
Define protection mechanisms: rate limits, quotas, circuit breakers, backpressure, authz checks and audit trails.
Define evolution strategy: schema changes, versioning, backfills, migrations and rollback.
Start with requirements and explicit assumptions instead of a memorized architecture.
Estimate scale quickly enough to identify the first bottleneck.
Draw the simplest working design, then harden it for scale, failures and operations.
State tradeoffs and rejected alternatives; this is where seniority is visible.

tradeoffs_to_be_able_to_explain: speed of interview progress vs depth
common_failure_modes: using Architecture decision records and design docs as a buzzword without showing concrete data/control flow
not showing how Architecture decision records and design docs behaves during overload or partial failure

diagrams_to_draw.candidate_prompt: Draw a sequence diagram for Architecture decision records and design docs. Include clients, edge, services, data stores, queues, caches, observability and the main failure path.

diagrams_to_draw.name: capacity flow diagram
diagrams_to_draw.purpose: Expose operational controls for Architecture decision records and design docs: health checks, alerts, fallbacks and rollback paths.

A strong answer explains when the technique is useful, when it fails, what it costs, and how the design changes as traffic, teams and reliability targets grow.
modules.role_application: In interviews, Event replay and reprocessing safety usually appears when the candidate must move from a vague product problem to an executable architecture. Use it to justify boundaries, choose data stores, define APIs, calculate scale, and explain the tradeoff between correctness, latency, availability, cost and team ownership.
reading_path: Start from the problem and user-visible requirements.
Quantify scale and reliability before choosing services.
Design the baseline architecture and explicitly name state ownership.
Stress the design with failures, overload, stale data, security threats and cost constraints.
Finalize with diagrams, metrics, migration path and open risks.

details: Define the problem that Event replay and reprocessing safety solves and the failure it prevents.

Trace retries, duplicate messages, stale reads, authorization failures, overload and regional failures.

Define ownership: team, service, database, on-call path and escalation path.
Define operational signals: golden metrics, logs, traces, saturation metrics and business KPIs.

Draw the simplest working design, then harden it for scale, failures and operations.

Study it by connecting requirements, scale assumptions, data ownership, failure behavior, security boundaries and operational controls. A strong answer explains when the technique is useful, when it fails, what it costs, and how the design changes as traffic, teams and reliability targets grow.
modules.role_application: In interviews, Orchestration vs choreography usually appears when the candidate must move from a vague product problem to an executable architecture. Use it to justify boundaries, choose data stores, define APIs, calculate scale, and explain the tradeoff between correctness, latency, availability, cost and team ownership.
reading_path: Start from the problem and user-visible requirements.
Quantify scale and reliability before choosing services.
Design the baseline architecture and explicitly name state ownership.
Stress the design with failures, overload, stale data, security threats and cost constraints.
Finalize with diagrams, metrics, migration path and open risks.

details: Define the problem that Orchestration vs choreography solves and the failure it prevents.
Identify the primary state owner, the scaling unit, and the consistency expectation.
Separate product invariants from implementation preferences before choosing technology.
Write the one-sentence tradeoff: what becomes easier and what becomes harder if you use this design.
Trace the happy path for Orchestration vs choreography from client request to durable state and response.
Trace retries, duplicate messages, stale reads, authorization failures, overload and regional failures.
Map every state change to a persistence, cache, queue, index or external dependency.
Connect each decision to one of the constraints: volume, latency, availability, correctness, security or cost.
Define ownership: team, service, database, on-call path and escalation path.
Define operational signals: golden metrics, logs, traces, saturation metrics and business KPIs.
Define protection mechanisms: rate limits, quotas, circuit breakers, backpressure, authz checks and audit trails.
Define evolution strategy: schema changes, versioning, backfills, migrations and rollback.
Start with requirements and explicit assumptions instead of a memorized architecture.
Estimate scale quickly enough to identify the first bottleneck.
Draw the simplest working design, then harden it for scale, failures and operations.
State tradeoffs and rejected alternatives; this is where seniority is visible.

tradeoffs_to_be_able_to_explain: synchronous composition vs async eventual consistency
common_failure_modes: using Orchestration vs choreography as a buzzword without showing concrete data/control flow
not showing how Orchestration vs choreography behaves during overload or partial failure

diagrams_to_draw.purpose: Show the boundaries, actors, dependencies and ownership model for Orchestration vs choreography.

diagrams_to_draw.name: C4 container diagram
diagrams_to_draw.purpose: Trace the critical request, data or control flow for Orchestration vs choreography, including failures and retries.
diagrams_to_draw.candidate_prompt: Draw a C4 container diagram for Orchestration vs choreography. Include clients, edge, services, data stores, queues, caches, observability and the main failure path.

diagrams_to_draw.name: service dependency graph
diagrams_to_draw.purpose: Make the scale, state, consistency or regional topology decisions for Orchestration vs choreography explicit.
diagrams_to_draw.candidate_prompt: Draw a service dependency graph for Orchestration vs choreography. Include clients, edge, services, data stores, queues, caches, observability and the main failure path.

diagrams_to_draw.name: workflow orchestration diagram
diagrams_to_draw.purpose: Expose operational controls for Orchestration vs choreography: health checks, alerts, fallbacks and rollback paths.
diagrams_to_draw.candidate_prompt: Draw a workflow orchestration diagram for Orchestration vs choreography. Include clients, edge, services, data stores, queues, caches, observability and the main failure path.

hands_on_labs: Build a design note for Orchestration vs choreography with assumptions, APIs, data model, capacity estimates and failure modes.
Draw the critical-path sequence diagram for Orchestration vs choreography; mark every synchronous call and timeout.
Run a scale-up exercise: increase traffic 100x and list which component fails first and why.
Write a postmortem scenario for Orchestration vs choreography: choose a realistic outage, root cause it, and modify the architecture.
practice_drills: Explain Orchestration vs choreography in 90 seconds to a staff engineer.
Explain Orchestration vs choreography in 90 seconds to a product manager without jargon.
Name three alternatives to the main approach and one reason each alternative may be better.
Choose one metric that proves Orchestration vs choreography is working and one metric that proves it is failing.
mastery_check: Can you draw Orchestration vs choreography from memory and explain every arrow?
Can you quantify how Orchestration vs choreography affects latency, storage, cost or availability?
Can you explain the migration path from a simpler design to this design?
Can you identify the worst failure mode and the first alert that would catch it?
Can you defend the design against an interviewer pushing for a different data store, API style or deployment model?
assessment_prompts: Design a production-ready subsystem where Orchestration vs choreography is the central design challenge.
Compare two designs for Orchestration vs choreography: one optimized for low latency and one optimized for correctness.
Given 10x traffic, 5x data size and one regional outage, revise the architecture for Orchestration vs choreography.
Find the hidden single point of failure in a proposed Orchestration vs choreography architecture.

study_notes: Service boundaries should follow ownership and data invariants, not random nouns.
Every boundary creates latency, coordination and operational cost.
Start simple and evolve only when scale or team structure requires it.
questions_to_answer_before_interview: What is the source of truth for Orchestration vs choreography?
Which operation becomes the bottleneck first for Orchestration vs choreography: read, write, fanout, storage, network, or coordination?
What are the exact consistency and freshness guarantees users need for Orchestration vs choreography?
How does Orchestration vs choreography behave when a dependency is slow, unavailable, overloaded, or returning partial errors?
Which metric, alert and dashboard would prove Orchestration vs choreography is healthy in production?
advanced_variations_to_practice: Orchestration vs choreography under 10x traffic
Orchestration vs choreography under a regional outage
Orchestration vs choreography with stricter privacy or compliance requirements
senior_level_signals: States assumptions and constraints before drawing.
Names rejected alternatives and explains why they were rejected.
Separates data plane, control plane and operational plane where relevant.
Designs for migration, rollback, observability and ownership.
Quantifies tradeoffs instead of saying it depends.
